clue.text: Where I see my Reds playing? (10)

definitions.text: Where I see my Reds playing?

indicators.note: Letters at play are larking about rather than standing still, so the ten in front of the word will not keep the order they were given.

blocks.note: the supporter's boast supplies exactly ten letters, and they are the ten needed

explanation.walkthrough: The Reds are Liverpool FC. The whole sentence works twice over: ask it as a question and it is also the material that answers it, which is why nothing is left over.
explanation.definitionFit: Liverpool play in red, and their metropolitan county is the stretch of north-west England around the river Mersey the question is asking about.

clue.text: Work together well, as Everyman quiet (4)

blocks.note: the setter's own name in this paper, so it stands for the first person
sh is the noise you make when asking for quiet

explanation.walkthrough: A setter writing themselves into their own clue is a standing Everyman trick, and 'as' is doing nothing but holding the sentence upright.
explanation.definitionFit: Gear teeth that mesh engage and turn each other smoothly, and the same verb is used of people who cooperate without friction.

clue.text: Piglet's friend, we hear, is basis for various sauces (4)

indicators.note: What is heard rather than read points at the noise a name makes, not the way it is spelt.

blocks.note: Roo is the small kangaroo of the Hundred Acre Wood, and his name is said exactly like the French cookery term

explanation.walkthrough: A A Milne supplies the friend; the kitchen supplies a French spelling that the sound gives no hint of. Everything turns on hearing the name rather than reading it.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the cooked paste of flour and fat that thickens bechamel, veloute and the rest, so it really is the base those sauces are started from.

clue.text: Beer, average (but free): I'm keen (5,6)

definitions.note: The answer is a noun for a person, while the definition is a whole clause — it is what such a person would say about themselves, not a word that swaps in for the phrase.

indicators.note: Letters set free are no longer held in the position they were handed to you in, so they may settle anywhere.

blocks.note: eleven letters of material; the comma is the setter's punctuation and counts for nothing

explanation.walkthrough: The bracket makes 'but free' read as a note on the bar prices, when it is the instruction that unsettles the eleven letters standing just before it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names somebody enthusiastic to the point of comedy, first into work and last out, so a first-person claim of keenness identifies them.

clue.text: Output of lawmaker investing time in public art (7)

indicators.note: To invest in something is to put money into it, and the same verb here puts one letter inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: a statue is the commonest piece of art standing in a public square
t is the standard abbreviation for time, as on a stopwatch

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a politician spending time on the arts budget, which is a good disguise. 'Output of lawmaker' means the law itself, not the person who drafts it.
explanation.definitionFit: A statute is a written law passed by a legislature, so it is precisely the product a lawmaker exists to turn out.

clue.text: Compadres denied bottles somewhere on the Elbe (7)

indicators.note: To bottle something is to seal it up inside glass, so what is wanted sits whole and unbroken within the words either side of it.

blocks.note: seven consecutive letters start in the middle of the first word and finish inside the second

explanation.walkthrough: 'Compadres' pulls hard towards Spanish and the answer is German, which is the whole disguise: a run of perfectly ordinary letters hides behind a word from the wrong country.
explanation.definitionFit: The city is the Saxon capital standing on the Elbe, so naming its river places it as surely as naming the country would.

clue.text: Man-eater correspondingly retires (4)

indicators.note: Somebody who retires withdraws, going back the way they came, and these four letters travel in the same direction.

blocks.note: 'correspondingly' is ergo, the logician's therefore, and those four letters are then read the other way round

explanation.walkthrough: Latin ergo is worth stocking up on: crosswords use it for 'therefore', 'so' and 'accordingly'. The surface, meanwhile, is a monster quietly taking his pension.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogre is the child-eating giant of folk tales, so the definition names him by the habit that makes him one.

clue.text: Sum that gives you a G? (5,5)

definitions.text: Sum that gives you a G?

blocks.note: the surface offers plain arithmetic, a column of figures waiting to be added up
the italic letter is slang for a thousand, so the figure at the bottom of the column is money and comes to exactly that

explanation.walkthrough: No letters move anywhere; the clue is one pun held together by the italics. Read the G as a musical note or a school grade and the whole thing stays shut.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the final figure once every subtotal is added in, and here that figure is a thousand — which is what the slang letter buys you.

clue.text: Archaeopteryx etc: their diet includes worms (5,5)

blocks.note: the Jurassic fossil usually called the first of the birds, with 'etc' widening it to the whole dawn group
the proverb hands the worm to whoever is up first, so the menu identifies the riser

explanation.walkthrough: One half is palaeontology and the other is a proverb about getting out of bed, with a colon the only thing between them. Not a single letter shifts.
explanation.definitionFit: Read of the first creatures to evolve into birds it is literal; read of the proverb's worm-catchers it is the everyday sense, people who rise before everyone else.

clue.text: Unedified attitude of our gross primate on board (4,6)

indicators.note: Anything carried on board is inside the vessel, so the ship's two letters close around everything else.

blocks.note: SS is the crossword's steamship, and being aboard puts the rest between its two letters
the clue's own word, taken exactly as it stands
gr. is the standard abbreviation for a gross, the twelve dozen of the wholesale trade
an ape is the primate a crossword reaches for first

explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a coarse monkey aboard a ship, which is the wrong picture entirely. The attitude is Aesop's: the fox decides the fruit he cannot reach was never worth having.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the pretence that what you failed to get was not worth wanting — an ungracious stance rather than an elevating one.

clue.text: Item that sounds like prune - or another fruit (4)

indicators.note: The phrase asks for the noise a word makes rather than its letters, and here two different words make the very same noise.

blocks.note: to prune a shrub is to pare it back, and pare is said this way
the pear is the second fruit, and it hides in the same single sound

explanation.walkthrough: One sound, three spellings: the clue hands you two of them and you write in the third. 'Item' is the couple sense, two people spoken of as one.
explanation.definitionFit: An item is a twosome, the couple everybody talks about as a unit, so the definition works on that sense and not on a thing in a list.

clue.text: Occasion celebrating pork mince - yet again? (9,3)

definitions.note: The answer is the name of a day, a noun, while the definition is adverbial — the film turned the name into a byword for an experience repeated without end.

blocks.note: minced meat is ground meat, the same operation under two names
pork comes off a hog, so the animal stands in for its meat
a big day is an occasion, as in 'the big day'
surface only: it makes the clue read as a food festival and carries no letters

explanation.walkthrough: A pork festival is a fine disguise for a February morning in Pennsylvania, where a rodent forecasts the spring and a film sent the same twenty-four hours round for ever.
explanation.definitionFit: The film left the phrase meaning a day that comes round unchanged, so the idiom is exactly a weary 'yet again' rather than a sense of the separate words.

clue.text: First mistake: milling grain in silo (8,3)

indicators.note: Grain sent through a mill comes out with no trace of the shape it went in with, and letters treated the same way land somewhere new.

blocks.note: eleven letters, the whole phrase going into the mill

explanation.walkthrough: Farm machinery on the surface, theology underneath. 'Milling' sits so comfortably beside grain that it barely reads as an instruction at all, which is the trap.
explanation.definitionFit: In Christian doctrine it is the first transgression, Adam and Eve's, that every later generation inherits — literally the earliest mistake there was.

clue.text: Predictor's remiss: that tells you something (10)

indicators.note: To be remiss is to be careless in your duty, and careless handling leaves the parts of a word out of their proper places.

blocks.note: ten letters, and the possessive S at the end is part of the material rather than grammar

explanation.walkthrough: 'Predictor's remiss' reads as a grumble about a forecaster who got it wrong, and that grumble is where every letter comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptor is a word or tag attached to a thing to convey what it is like, so it is a label whose only job is to inform you.

clue.text: Emphasise cricket match is trial demanding endurance (6,4)

blocks.note: to stress a word is to emphasise it
a Test is an international cricket match between two countries, played over five days

explanation.walkthrough: Banks and hearts get put through these; the surface offers five days in the sun instead. Test cricket is worth knowing, because setters use it for any kind of trial.
explanation.definitionFit: A stress test loads something until it shows where it gives way, so both the engineering and the medical kind are trials of how much can be borne.

clue.text: Kiss in cemetery, naked, dancing: it's a bit much (7)

indicators.note: A word stripped naked loses what it wears on the outside, so the first and last letters come off and the middle is left standing.
Dancers keep swapping places about the floor, and letters told to dance do exactly the same.

blocks.note: CEMETERY with its outer C and Y taken off leaves six letters
X is the kiss written at the foot of a letter

explanation.walkthrough: The graveyard and the dancing belong to the surface's ghost story. The definition is the small phrase at the end, which reads like part of that story and is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling something a bit much is British understatement for excessive, and the answer is the plain word for going that far past the middle.

clue.text: Flipping interminable, the writer wearies Scotsman somewhere in Kenya (7)

indicators.note: To flip something is to turn it over end for end, so the assembled letters are read the opposite way round.
Something interminable has no end, so the word it governs is written without its final letter.

blocks.note: the person writing the clue refers to themselves as I
to weary somebody is to bore them, and the last letter of that verb is dropped
Ian is the Scottish forename crosswords keep permanently on hand

explanation.walkthrough: Built in clue order the wordplay spells out a tedious Scot, and only turning the whole assembly round produces an African capital. 'Flipping' is doing duty as mild swearing too.
explanation.definitionFit: The city is Kenya's capital and by far its largest, so the definition locates it by country and leaves you to supply the name.

clue.text: Butcher, vilified, hides leaves (7)

indicators.note: Something hidden is present but not shown, so what is wanted is already there in the clue, untouched and in order.

blocks.note: seven consecutive letters begin at the fourth letter of the first word and run on into the second

explanation.walkthrough: A butcher being vilified is a strong enough picture to hide a herb behind. The herb is the salad kind, fine feathery fronds used much as parsley is.
explanation.definitionFit: Chervil is a delicate herb grown for its foliage, so naming the part that reaches the kitchen names the plant itself.

clue.text: Monarch and family switching sides to gain allegiance (7)

indicators.note: Left and right are the two sides on offer, and switching them takes out the letter that stands for one and puts in the letter for the other.

blocks.note: royalty is the reigning house, the monarch together with their relatives
the R that opens that word is right, and left puts an L in its place

explanation.walkthrough: Switching sides normally means the opposite of what is being defined, which is the joke: change one letter of the royal household and out comes the very virtue a turncoat lacks.
explanation.definitionFit: Allegiance is the faithfulness owed to a person or cause, so the two are near-exact synonyms, one out of feudal French and one plainer.

clue.text: Highway robber's sturdy as well as round: right! (7)

indicators.note: To go round something is to enclose it, so the word just clued closes over the letter that comes next.

blocks.note: a big man is a sturdy one, the same solid build
r is the standard abbreviation for right, as in stage directions
'as well as' joins two things exactly as the conjunction does

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark makes 'right!' sound like a cry of agreement, which is why it reads as surface rather than as the single letter it is.
explanation.definitionFit: A brigand is one of a band of robbers who prey on travellers, so a robber working the highway is the plain historical sense.

clue.text: Helpful youngster baked something that's chewy (7)

blocks.note: the junior branch of the Guides, girls of about seven to ten, known for doing a good turn daily
the dense chocolate square cut from a tray, deliberately underdone so it stays soft

explanation.walkthrough: A British uniformed movement and an American tray-bake, sharing one spelling and nothing else. No letters move; you simply have to hear the word twice.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the small girl in uniform doing her good deed, the other the chocolate square from the tin — the same word in two unrelated traditions.

clue.text: Or is my story a shambles, sadly? (2,5,2,3)

indicators.note: A shambles is a scene of total disorder, where nothing at all is standing where it ought to be.

blocks.note: twelve letters, the whole opening of the clue including its small 'a'

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a writer's anxious question about their own manuscript, and every word of it except the last is material. Only 'sadly' is doing the defining.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are ways of flagging a regrettable fact as you report it, so the adverb stands in for the polite formula that softens the same bad news.

clue.text: Yes, Russian getting UK newspaper is ridiculous (4)

blocks.note: da is the Russian for yes
the FT is the Financial Times, the pink-papered London business daily

explanation.walkthrough: Two abbreviations from very different worlds laid end to end, with a Russian buying a British paper as the cover story that keeps the join out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Daft is the everyday British word for silly or absurd, so 'ridiculous' is the same idea pitched a little more formally.

clue.text: Moneyed European's resplendent carrier, primarily? (4)

indicators.note: What comes primarily comes first, so each word in front of it gives up only the letter it begins with.

blocks.note: four words standing in a row, each handing over its first letter

explanation.walkthrough: Read once, the sentence is an instruction about initials; read again, it describes the car those initials spell — a German marque, expensive and gleaming.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the familiar British short form of Mercedes, and the whole clue describes one: a costly, shining vehicle from a European maker.

clue.text: Like shoelaces needing extra time (4)

blocks.note: laces are knotted in a bow at the top of the shoe, which is the everyday sense
a cup match still level after ninety minutes goes to extra time, which is the sporting sense

explanation.walkthrough: One definition is a bow on a shoe and the other a scoreline at the final whistle. Four letters cover both, and not one of them moves.
explanation.definitionFit: The shoelace sense is fastened with a knot; the football sense is level on goals with the match undecided — one word for a knot and for a draw.

clue.text: Fresh start; military dummies behind schedule (5,5)

blocks.note: blanks are the cartridges fired on exercise, charged but with no bullet in them
running behind schedule is simply being late

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an army exercise that has overrun. The answer reaches back to the schoolroom: a writing slate wiped clean, with nothing yet chalked on it.
explanation.definitionFit: A blank slate is a state with nothing recorded on it yet, which is exactly what anyone beginning over again is handed.

clue.text: Spoil a list of duties (4)

blocks.note: food left out will spoil, which is to rot
the clue's own word, carried straight across

explanation.walkthrough: In British workplaces this is the sheet pinned to the wall saying whose turn it is next: the washing-up, the school run, the night shift.
explanation.definitionFit: A rota is the roster setting out who performs which duty and when, so the definition names it by precisely what it lists.

clue.text: Britain restrained by unwise reticency regarding futuristic tech (10)

indicators.note: An unwise arrangement is one nobody would have chosen deliberately, and these letters end up in exactly such an order.
To be restrained by something is to be held inside it, so the single letter goes within the material rather than alongside it.

blocks.note: B is the standard abbreviation for Britain, as on the old oval car plates
nine letters from a rare form of reticence, holding your tongue

explanation.walkthrough: 'Reticency' is a real if unusual word, and its oddity is the tell: a word that sits awkwardly in the surface is generally there for its letters alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective belongs to the study of automatic control and communication in machines, the vocabulary of robots and feedback loops.
